title: Indian PhD Couple Wins $200,000 Settlement Over 'Food Racism' at University of Colorado
excerpt: Aditya Prakash and Urmi Bhattacheryya alleged systemic discrimination after a staff member objected to the smell of palak paneer being reheated in a shared microwave.
body:
• Two Indian PhD students at the University of Colorado Boulder won a $200,000 civil rights settlement after alleging discrimination that began when a staff member called their palak paneer "pungent."
  • Aditya Prakash and Urmi Bhattacheryya said the microwave dispute escalated into retaliation, including loss of teaching roles, withheld master's degrees, and eventual loss of doctoral funding.
  • The university denied liability but agreed to pay the settlement and confer both students' master's degrees as part of the September 2025 agreement.
  • The couple has returned to India and is permanently barred from future enrollment or employment at the university.

A Microwave Dispute That Became a Federal Lawsuit

It started with lunch. On September 5, 2023, Aditya Prakash, a PhD student in anthropology at the University of Colorado Boulder, placed a bowl of palak paneer — a common Indian spinach and cheese dish — into a shared departmental microwave. An administrative assistant objected to the smell, calling it "pungent" and telling Prakash not to use the microwave for strong-smelling food.

"It's just food. I'm heating and leaving," Prakash told the staff member, according to his account to The Indian Express. He declined to comply.

What followed, the couple alleges, was not a disagreement about office etiquette. It was the start of two years of escalating retaliation that would strip them of their academic careers and drive them out of the country.

From Complaint to Retaliation

Two days after the microwave incident, Prakash and four other students — including his partner, Urmi Bhattacheryya, also pursuing a PhD in cultural anthropology — heated Indian food in the same microwave in what they described as a quiet act of protest.

The department responded with a campus-wide email asking members to avoid preparing food with "strong or lingering smells." Prakash replied to all, calling the suggestion discriminatory and pointing out that a staff member had previously heated chili in a crockpot in the same office without complaint.

> **"An administrative assistant objected to the smell, calling it "pungent" and telling Prakash not to use the microwave for strong-smelling food.

"It's just food."**

"How many groups of people do you know that face racism on a daily basis because they eat broccoli?"

— Aditya Prakash, responding to a faculty member who suggested broccoli would also be inappropriate

Prakash was subsequently summoned to repeated meetings with senior faculty and accused of making the staff member "feel unsafe." Complaints were filed against him with the Office of Student Conduct. Bhattacheryya, 35, lost her teaching assistantship without warning or explanation. When she and other students later brought Indian food to campus, they were accused of inciting a riot — an allegation that was later dismissed.

The department then refused to grant either student their master's degrees, which PhD students at the university typically receive along the way to their doctorate. Both were eventually cited for poor performance and lost their doctoral funding entirely.

![The Indian Express — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/8/85/Indian-Expree.jpg)

The Legal Battle

In May 2025, Prakash and Bhattacheryya filed a federal civil rights lawsuit in the United States District Court for the District of Colorado, alleging discrimination and retaliation. The suit argued that the university's response to the food complaint reflected deeper systemic bias against international students.

By September 2025, the University of Colorado Boulder agreed to settle. The terms: $200,000 paid to the couple and the conferral of both their master's degrees. In exchange, both students are permanently barred from future enrollment or employment at the university. The university denied any liability.

"The university reached an agreement with the plaintiffs and denies any liability," university spokesperson Deborah Mendez Wilson said in a statement. "CU Boulder remains committed to fostering an inclusive environment for students, faculty and staff."

A Broader Pattern for Indian Students Abroad

The case has resonated widely among Indian diaspora communities, tapping into a familiar experience: the policing of cultural practices — particularly food — in Western academic and professional spaces. Complaints about the smell of Indian cooking in shared kitchens and offices are a recurring grievance among South Asian immigrants.

"Acts of isolating by my classmates or stopping me from using a shared microwave because of how my food smells are how white people control your Indianness and shrink the spaces you can exist in."

— Aditya Prakash, to the BBC

Bhattacheryya linked the hostility to a broader political climate. "There is a narrowing of empathy. Discomfort is tolerated less, especially when it comes from immigrants or people of color," she told The Indian Express.

Prakash, a native of Bhopal, and Bhattacheryya, from Kolkata, first met in Delhi before enrolling for PhDs in the United States. They returned to India in January 2026 and are now engaged.

What It Means Going Forward

While the settlement resolves the immediate legal dispute, the case raises unresolved questions about how universities handle complaints that intersect cultural identity and institutional power. Discrimination that begins with food — something deeply tied to cultural identity — can serve as a proxy for broader exclusion.

Prakash told the BBC he likely will not return to the United States. "No matter how good you are at what you do, the system is constantly telling you that because of your skin colour or your nationality, you can be sent back any time," he said.

The case has drawn coverage from The New York Times, BBC, The Indian Express, and India-West, becoming one of the most widely discussed discrimination cases involving Indian students in recent years.
